title: Fools Will Resign!!!
reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later boards reviewed. Begin after ...Qd6 at 155 seconds in the complete nine-piece later diagram: White Kc2/Ra5/Nd4/c3/e4 against Ke7/Qd6/c4/f6. Nf5+ is certified against every legal Black reply and subsequent defense, reaching exact seven-piece wins by the knight/queen exchange or the c4 pawn capture. The source Ke6/Nxd6/Kxd6 ending is shown; the Kd7/Kc6/Nxc4 completion is explicitly independent. Earlier Rc8/queen chase/king shepherd and Ra5 choices remain outside this proof. Native diagrams correct the earlier provisional Kb2 identification to Kc2.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players will make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to find the incredible win that white has in this position. It might seem like there's no way to make any progress because the black queen will always be able to outplay this white rook and this white knight. [music] But white has an incredible resource in this position. And the first very important move that white needs to find in this position is the brilliant rook to c8. Sacrificing a full rook. But of course the rook is untouchable because if the queen takes it, now there would be a knight fork winning the queen and the game. But if we pay close attention, we notice that this queen doesn't have many squares to go to. All of these are covered by the knight here and here. If the queen goes to this square, there is going to be another fork. This is defended by the rook and this is defended by the pawn leaving the black queen with the only option to go to a3. But this is not a problem for black. He's going to follow up with something like queen to a2 check. Simply escape with the queen. And now this would be an easy draw if not a win. But see, the knight and rook complement each other. And if they find [music] the right harmony, they can outplay this black queen. Now white follows up with knight to b4 check. Now of course if the king ever steps to this line, this rook check is going to skewer the king and queen and win the queen. But the king can simply go up. Now white follows up with rook to b8 check. It seems like white is desperately trying to deliver any check available in the position. But of course, if the king goes here, there is going to be a fork. And the same thing happens if the king goes here. So the black king is forced to go to c5. Now white keeps going with his apparent king hunt with rook to b5. This time the king only has one square on d6. And it seems like black is simply out of the woods. But that is not the case. White is not done. And he follows up with rook to d5 check. And we can now start to see the brilliant idea of white. First of all, the king cannot go this way again because of a fork. And all of these squares are covered by the white pieces leaving black with only king to e7. We have pushed the king to the other side of the board and brought the queen to this side. What for? Well, white had seen the incredible [music] and beautiful rook a5. It's the same sacrificial idea. The queen cannot take because of a fork. But this time it's much more powerful. The queen doesn't actually have any safe squares to go to leaving as the only option the d6 square. But as you can imagine, white has a fork with the knight. He's going to pick up the queen and win this game. If you want to improve at chess, I suggest you download Chess Mind the AI. An AI-powered chess training program like no other. Check it out.
